plan.summary: Quick-mode, 12-month review of MSFT as of 2026-09-17 answering three operator questions: (1) is cloud margin expansion economic or an artefact of capitalising infrastructure, (2) what must be true for the current multiple, (3) how much growth is AI revenue absent in FY2023. This plan states no figures; all numbers come from filed evidence and recorded calculations. Revised after review to add: ASC 606 revenue disaggregation, unearned revenue and remaining performance obligations (with disclosed recognition split) as the durability test; explicit enterprise-value bridge inputs (cash and short-term investments, total debt, operating and finance lease liabilities, equity-method carrying values, diluted share count, buybacks, stock-based compensation); a pre-committed reverse-DCF solve protocol so 'what would have to be true' is falsifiable; a fallback rule when no cloud-level operating margin is disclosed; and core/optional source tiering. Optional sources (peer 10-Ks, DEF 14A, full transcript series) are dropped before any core retrieval is abbreviated. Sections below are ordered by priority under a time box.

challenges.statement: The 10-K source entry lists income statement, segment, PP&E, lease, cash flow, commitments and cover page — but not the ASC 606 revenue disaggregation note, unearned revenue, or remaining performance obligations and their expected recognition period. Neither is planned.

sections.focus: Direct answers to the three operator questions, each tagged with its evidence class (audited filing, unaudited company disclosure, management assertion, unverified proposal). Where filings cannot settle a question, say so plainly: if no cloud-level operating margin is derivable from segment disclosure, state that it was not derivable rather than constructing one; if no audited AI revenue line exists, say the question is bounded, not resolved. Name the variables held fixed in the reverse DCF and where their values came from. Carry forward the single largest disagreement surfaced by validation.

FY2023-FY2026 consolidated and segment revenue, operating income and margin from the 10-Ks, as-reported and recast where disclosed. Retrieve the ASC 606 revenue disaggregation by product/service line as the closest audited proxy for which lines could contain AI offerings. Durability test: track remaining performance obligations and unearned revenue growth, with disclosed recognition-period split, against reported revenue growth across the same years. Fallback rule: if no cloud-level operating margin is disclosed, report reportable-segment margin as presented plus any company-defined Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage, labelled unaudited. Core of the capitalisation question. Operating cash flow, additions to property and equipment, finance-lease additions, non-cash depreciation, stock-based compensation and share repurchases from FY2024-FY2026 cash flow statements and FY2026 10-Qs. Compare capex growth with depreciation growth and with reported cloud-related revenue growth to test whether margin leads or lags the cash cost of capacity. Show the quarterly trajectory annual figures smooth over. Record explicitly where filings do not split datacentre shell, land, leased capacity and server spend.

Reverse DCF of implied expectations, not a fair value. Pre-committed solve protocol: hold discount rate (date-stamped Treasury yield plus a documented ERP source) and terminal growth fixed at sourced values; fix capex intensity and operating margin at the most recent disclosed period levels; solve for one variable at a time and report a stated grid with every held value and its source named. Diluted shares govern; use the most recent date-stamped count available and disclose its date versus 2026-09-17. Note terminal value dominance versus the 12-month horizon.

Two jobs. First, the capitalised-infrastructure question: gross and net property and equipment, accumulated depreciation, construction in progress, disclosed useful lives, and operating versus finance lease liabilities and maturities from the FY2026 10-K notes, establishing how much infrastructure cost sits on the balance sheet awaiting depreciation. Second, supply the enterprise-value bridge items to valuation_dcf: cash and short-term investments, total and current debt with maturities, lease liabilities, and equity-method or unconsolidated investments with related commitments that sit outside consolidated margin.

Define reportable segments exactly as presented in the FY2026 10-K segment note and identify every recast or reallocation versus FY2023-FY2025 presentation, since comparability is the crux of the AI-growth question. Map the ASC 606 disaggregation categories to segments and identify which disclosed revenue lines could contain AI offerings. Mark which metrics (Microsoft Cloud revenue, Azure growth rates, any AI run-rate) are company-defined, non-GAAP or unaudited, and note that no reportable segment maps one-to-one to 'Microsoft Cloud'.

State the thesis as falsifiable conditions over the 12-month horizon, each linked to the filing line or note that would confirm or break it at the next two reporting dates: direction of reportable-segment operating margin (or the fallback metric if no cloud margin is disclosed), capex-to-revenue trajectory, depreciation growth relative to segment revenue growth, remaining performance obligation growth relative to reported revenue growth, and whether AI-related revenue disclosure improves. No price target.

Risks to the investment case, ordered by materiality to the three operator questions: depreciation catch-up as capacity vintages mature, disclosed capex and purchase commitments, counterparty or customer concentration in AI arrangements, economics held in equity-method or unconsolidated vehicles, and disclosure risk if segment or metric definitions change again. themes.label: AI infrastructure capital expenditure buildout
themes.rationale: Microsoft is spending tens of billions annually on data centers and AI accelerators to support Azure and Copilot demand, directly driving capex intensity, depreciation growth, and free cash flow compression versus prior cloud-only capex cycles.

themes.label: Enterprise cloud migration and hyperscaler spend
themes.rationale: Azure's growth is tied to enterprise workload migration off on-premise systems; this secular shift underpins Microsoft's largest growth segment and links it to peers competing for the same enterprise IT budgets.

themes.label: Grid electrification and power constraints from datacenter demand
themes.rationale: Microsoft's data center buildout is a major driver of new electricity demand and grid investment, exposing it to power availability, pricing, and utility partnership constraints that could throttle capacity expansion.

themes.label: Generative AI enterprise monetization
themes.rationale: Microsoft's Copilot and OpenAI partnership represent a bet that generative AI features can be monetized across Office, GitHub, and Azure, a theme shared with other software vendors racing to justify AI investment via seat and usage revenue.

themes.label: AI hardware depreciation and useful-life risk
themes.rationale: Rapid GPU/accelerator obsolescence raises questions about depreciation schedules and asset useful lives for Microsoft's AI infrastructure, a risk factor increasingly scrutinized across all large AI capex spenders.

This rising finance-lease interest burden means Microsoft's massive AI/datacenter capex program has growing sensitivity to prevailing interest rates on lease and debt financing, since a larger share of its infrastructure is now leased/financed rather than owned outright — a macro (rates) linkage specific to its AI capex strategy.

Microsoft's Q4 FY26 results describe demand-side momentum directly tied to AI/cloud investment: Azure and other cloud services revenue grew 43% and Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $59.3B (+27%), with commercial remaining performance obligation up 84% to $678B, evidencing that enterprise AI/cloud capital spending is the dominant demand driver behind Microsoft's growth this cycle.

Other income (expense), net swung from -$4,901M in FY25 to +$10,697M in FY26, driven substantially by investment gains/losses on OpenAI and Anthropic stakes (e.g., a $3.2B Q4 gain from Anthropic), showing Microsoft's reported earnings are now materially exposed to swings in venture/equity-method investment valuations tied to AI-sector sentiment rather than traditional operating macro factors.

assumptions.name: exit_multiple
assumptions.justification: Cross-check, not an independent view: at ~8-9% WACC and 3% growth, a terminal FCF/EBITDA of roughly two-thirds implies low-teens EV/EBITDA. That conversion reflects the derived 44% EBIT margin plus ~9% D&A intensity, less tax at 17.5% and capex settling near D&A — the derived 20% capex intensity (35% in FY26) is a buildout, not a steady state. Current MSFT trades well above this on spot EBITDA; the gap is growth I do not extend into perpetuity. The perpetuity-growth terminal value is the better estimate; treat 13x as a sanity band. Higher if terminal capex stays near D&A and rates fall; lower if leased AI capacity keeps capex above depreciation.

assumptions.name: revenue_growth
assumptions.justification: The compound annual growth rate of revenue from 2022-06-30 to 2026-06-30, over 4 year(s): revenue moved from 198,270,000,000 to 331,839,000,000. Held flat across the forecast, because a trailing rate is one number and projecting a fade is a judgement this derivation does not make.

assumptions.justification: The US 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield was 5% on 2026-09-15, as published by 2026-09-17 (Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (H.15), series DGS10). Taken as the USD risk-free rate for this run's as-of date and converted to the fraction 0.05.

assumptions.name: terminal_growth
assumptions.justification: Taken as below a cost of capital of at least 8% (the derived 5% risk-free plus any ordinary equity premium for a beta-near-1 megacap), so it sits far under the eventual WACC. 3% is roughly long-run US nominal GDP at a 5% nominal 10-year yield: in perpetuity a company this large cannot exceed the economy, so I anchor there rather than on the derived 13.7% trailing growth or 43% Azure growth, which are cycle facts, not perpetuity facts. Raise toward 0.035 if you judge AI-era pricing power durable; cut to 0.02 if you assume nominal rates and nominal GDP fall back.

assumptions.name: working_capital_intensity
assumptions.justification: The mean of net working capital — current assets less current liabilities — over revenue, across 5 period(s) ending 2022-06-30, 2023-06-30, 2024-06-30, 2025-06-30, 2026-06-30. A negative figure is normal for a business paid before it pays, and is proposed as it stands rather than floored at zero.

caveats: Book equity was used as the equity weight because no market capitalisation was available. Book value is what the shares were issued and retained for rather than what they are worth, and for a profitable company it is usually far lower — so the equity weight is understated, the debt weight overstated, and the resulting WACC too low. Every valuation discounted at it is correspondingly too high.

More than three quarters of the enterprise value is terminal value. The explicit forecast is contributing little, so the answer rests almost entirely on the terminal assumption rather than on the projected years a reader can check.

The two terminal methods disagree by more than a quarter. That is information, not an error: they are two different guesses about the same unknowable quantity, and the distance between them is the honest width of the answer.

The bridge from enterprise value to equity value is net debt alone. Associate holdings, minority interests and pension deficits are not read off the filings by this build, so a business carrying material non-operating items is valued as though it does not.
